title: Time to first spike
summary: The message can be when the first spike happens, not how many follow.

terms.definition: A code in which the times of spikes, not only their count, carry the signal.

terms.plain: the clock time of the first spike
terms.definition: Also called latency coding. A stronger input makes the first spike earlier.
Random variation in spike time. Too much jitter washes a latency code out.

cards.text:
A strong input can fire the first spike early.
A weak input fires it late. The count may be one either way.

lines: The strong input spikes at 4 ms.
The weak input spikes at 15 ms.

question.prompt: In time-to-first-spike coding, which input was stronger?
question.why: Latency coding reads the clock. Sooner is stronger.
question.simpler: Ignore the count. Compare the first-spike times.

question.prompt: Large jitter makes a latency code easier to read.
question.why: Jitter scrambles the time that was supposed to carry the message.
question.simpler: A latency code needs the first spike to land near the time you meant.

recall.question: In latency coding, does a stronger input spike earlier or later?

deeper.note: Thorpe, Fize, and Marlot timed human visual categorization and argued the first spikes have to carry a lot, because a long count does not fit in the time available.

paper.title: Speed of processing in the human visual system
paper.section: The timing constraint on visual codes.
